documents.plain_text: # vitess-topo-monitor Watch a Vitess cluster's shard topology, replication lag and failover history, and alert the moment the live topology drifts from the one you declared. [![CI](https://github.com/sharded-topology/vitess-topo-monitor/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/sharded-topology/vitess-topo-monitor/actions/workflows/ci.yml) [![License: MIT](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-MIT-blue.svg)](LICENSE) [![Python 3.11+](https://img.shields.io/badge/python-3.11%20%7C%203.12%20%7C%203.13-blue.svg)](https://www.python.org/downloads/) ![The vitess-topo-monitor dashboard showing three keyspaces, a key-range coverage bar for each, per-shard health cards with replication-lag sparklines, an alerts panel listing four warnings, and a failover timeline](docs/dashboard.png) The same dashboard in dark theme: ![The same dashboard rendered in the dark theme](docs/dashboard-dark.png) Both screenshots are real captures of the dashboard running against the bundled offline fixture — you can reproduce them in about ten seconds with the quickstart below. --- ## What it does A Vitess keyspace is only correct if its shards **tile the key space exactly once**. `-40`, `40-80`, `80-c0`, `c0-` is a valid four-way split; drop one shard and every query for those keyspace IDs has nowhere to route. That invariant, plus "every shard has exactly one primary, in the cell you expect, with enough healthy replicas behind it, all within their lag budget", is what most Vitess incidents come down to — and none of it is visible in a single place. `vitess-topo-monitor` makes that invariant explicit. You write down the topology you *want* in YAML. The tool reads the topology you *have* from `vtctldclient` and Prometheus, compares them, and produces typed findings: ``` [x] KEYRANGE_GAP commerce commerce: key range 40-80 is not served by any shard [x] NO_PRIMARY commerce/80-c0 shard commerce/80-c0 has no elected primary [!] PRIMARY_WRONG_CELL commerce/c0- shard commerce/c0- primary is in cell zone2 ``` Each finding carries a stable code, a severity, an explanation, and a link to the page in the [Sharded Topology field guide](https://www.shardedtopology.org) that explains the underlying concept. The same analysis drives four surfaces: | Surface | What it is for | | --- | --- | | `vtmon check` | one-shot check for CI and cron; exit code encodes the worst severity | | `vtmon serve` | a live dashboard with coverage bars, health cards and a failover timeline | | `/metrics` | the findings re-exported as Prometheus gauges, so they feed real alerting | | `vtmon alerts` | render or dispatch alerts to stdout, a webhook, or Slack | ### Why it exists Vitess exposes plenty of metrics and `vtctldclient` exposes plenty of topology, but nothing connects the two to a written-down intent. `vttablet_replication_lag_seconds` tells you a replica is behind; it does not tell you that the shard is now one tablet away from having no promotion candidate, or that a Reshard cutover left a hole in your key space three hours ago. Drift detection needs a declaration to compare against, and that is the piece this tool adds. ## Install & quickstart There is no package index release. Clone the repository and work from the checkout: ```bash git clone https://github.com/sharded-topology/vitess-topo-monitor.git cd vitess-topo-monitor python -m venv .venv .venv/bin/pip install -r requirements.txt ``` Everything below runs **entirely offline** against the bundled fixtures — no Vitess, no Prometheus, no network. ```bash # 1. Check a healthy recorded cluster against the declaration. .venv/bin/python -m vtmon check \ -d examples/desired-topology.yaml \ --fixture examples/healthy-snapshot.json # 2. Check a degraded one (exits 2). .venv/bin/python -m vtmon check \ -d examples/desired-topology.yaml \ --fixture examples/drifted-snapshot.json # 3. Run the dashboard. .venv/bin/python -m vtmon serve \ -d examples/desired-topology.yaml \ --fixture examples/cluster-snapshot.json # then open http://127.0.0.1:8477/ ``` Against a real cluster, swap the fixture for a live source: ```bash .venv/bin/python -m vtmon serve \ -d topology.yaml \ --vtctld localhost:15999 \ --prometheus http://prometheus.internal:9090 ``` ## The declaration `examples/desired-topology.yaml`, abridged: ```yaml version: 1 defaults: slo: max_replication_lag_seconds: 30 min_healthy_replicas: 2 max_scatter_query_ratio: 0.15 max_reparents_in_window: 3 reparent_window_seconds: 3600 keyspaces: - name: commerce sharded: true cells: [zone1, zone2] shards: - name: "-40" tablets: zone1: {primary: 1, replica: 2, rdonly: 1} zone2: {replica: 1} - name: "40-80" tablets: zone1: {primary: 1, replica: 2, rdonly: 1} zone2: {replica: 1} # ... 80-c0, c0- ... - name: "c0-" tablets: zone1: {primary: 1, replica: 2, rdonly: 1} zone2: {replica: 1} slo: max_scatter_query_ratio: 0.20 # this shard fans out more max_replication_lag_seconds: 20 - name: lookup sharded: false cells: [zone1] shards: - name: "-" tablets: zone1: {primary: 1, replica: 1} ``` SLOs cascade: `defaults.slo` → `keyspaces[].slo` → `shards[].slo`, each level overriding only the fields it names. Validation is deliberately strict, because a declaration that cannot be satisfied is a bug in the declaration rather than drift in the cluster. Loading fails outright if: - a shard name is not a parseable Vitess key range (`-80`, `40-80`, `c0-`, `-`); - the shards of a sharded keyspace leave a gap or overlap; - an unsharded keyspace declares anything other than one full-range shard; - a shard declares more than one primary, a negative tablet count, an unknown tablet type, or a cell the keyspace does not list. ## How it works ### Key ranges Shard names are parsed into half-open byte ranges `[start, end)`. Boundaries are compared with right zero-padding to eight bytes, which is how Vitess's own `key.KeyRange` comparison works, so `80` and `8000` are the same boundary. Coverage analysis sorts the ranges, walks them once looking for gaps, and does a pairwise sweep for overlaps. A perfect partition produces no problems; anything else produces one `CoverageProblem` per offending span, which becomes a `KEYRANGE_GAP` or `KEYRANGE_OVERLAP` finding. Coverage is computed over **serving** shards only. A shard with `is_primary_serving=false` is deliberately treated as absent, because that is exactly how VTGate treats it — which is why a Reshard cutover shows up as both `SHARD_NOT_SERVING` and a temporary gap. ### Collectors Everything that touches a cluster sits behind one interface: ```python class Collector(abc.ABC): @abc.abstractmethod def collect(self) -> Snapshot: ... ``` Three implementations ship: - **`FixtureCollector`** replays a recorded JSON snapshot. A fixture may hold one document or a list of them; with a list, successive `collect()` calls walk forward and then hold on the last frame, which is how the offline demo animates lag and produces a failover timeline with no infrastructure at all. **This is the default and the path the tests exercise.** - **`VtctldCollector`** shells out to `vtctldclient` — `GetKeyspaces`, `FindAllShardsInKeyspace ` and `GetTablets`, all with `--json`. It shells out rather than speaking gRPC so it inherits whatever authentication your `vtctldclient` already has. The output is protobuf-JSON, whose field names appear as either `snake_case` or `lowerCamelCase` depending on the build, so both spellings are accepted. Tablet types this tool does not model (`BACKUP`, `DRAINED`, `RESTORE`, `SPARE`, `EXPERIMENTAL`) are skipped rather than guessed at. - **`PrometheusCollector`** *decorates* one of the others. Topology facts come from the topology server; health facts come from Prometheus, joined back onto tablets by the `keyspace`/`shard`/`alias` labels. A query that fails becomes a note on the snapshot rather than an exception, so a Prometheus outage degrades the report instead of killing it. #### Which Vitess version's metric names? The default PromQL targets **Vitess v20/v21**, scraped from the standard `/metrics` endpoint with `--emit_stats --stats_backend prometheus`: | Purpose | Default PromQL | | --- | --- | | Replica replication lag | `vttablet_replication_lag_seconds` | | Throttler check activity | `vttablet_throttler_check_any_total` | | Scatter query rate | `rate(vtgate_queries_processed{Plan="Scatter"}[5m])` | | Total query rate | `rate(vtgate_queries_processed[5m])` | Metric names have changed across Vitess major versions, and different deployments relabel differently, so **every query is overridable** — `--promql-lag`, `--promql-throttler`, `--promql-scatter`, `--promql-total`. If your series are named differently, point the flags at yours; nothing else in the tool assumes a particular name. See [key VTTablet Prometheus metrics to watch](https://www.shardedtopology.org/observability-operations-for-sharded-vitess/monitoring-replication-lag-and-throttling/key-vttablet-prometheus-metrics-to-watch/) for what each of these actually measures. ### Reparent tracking Failovers are derived from two independent signals and merged: 1. **Snapshot diffing** — the primary alias for a shard differs between consecutive snapshots. 2. **Primary term start** — `primary_term_start_time`, which Vitess bumps on every successful `PlannedReparentShard` / `EmergencyReparentShard`. This catches a reparent even from a single snapshot, and catches the case where a shard reparented *back* to the same tablet. Events are deduplicated on `(shard, new primary, term start)`, so replaying overlapping windows never double-counts. A shard with at least `max_reparents_in_window` events inside `reparent_window_seconds` raises `REPARENT_FLAPPING` (critical) instead of the ordinary `RECENT_REPARENT` notice. ### Finding codes | Code | Severity | Meaning | | --- | --- | --- | | `KEYSPACE_MISSING` | critical | a declared keyspace is absent from topo | | `SHARD_MISSING` | critical | a declared shard is absent from topo | | `KEYRANGE_GAP` | critical | part of the key space is unserved | | `KEYRANGE_OVERLAP` | critical | two serving shards claim the same keys | | `SHARD_NOT_SERVING` | critical | `is_primary_serving` is false | | `NO_PRIMARY` | critical | no PRIMARY tablet for the shard | | `MULTIPLE_PRIMARIES` | critical | more than one PRIMARY tablet (split brain) | | `PRIMARY_NOT_SERVING` | critical | the primary record exists but is not serving | | `REPLICA_COUNT_LOW` | critical | healthy replicas below the SLO minimum | | `REPARENT_FLAPPING` | critical | too many reparents inside the window | | `SHARD_UNDECLARED` | warning | topo has a shard the declaration does not | | `PRIMARY_WRONG_CELL` | warning | primary sits outside its declared cells | | `TABLET_COUNT_MISMATCH` | warning | per-cell tablet counts differ from declared | | `REPLICATION_LAG_HIGH` | warning | replica lag over the SLO | | `TABLET_NOT_SERVING` | warning | a tablet is in a non-serving state | | `THROTTLER_CLOSED` | warning | throttler closed while lag is healthy | | `SCATTER_RATIO_HIGH` | warning | scatter-query ratio over the SLO | | `REPLICATION_LAG_UNKNOWN` | info | no lag metric for a serving replica | | `THROTTLER_OPEN` | info | throttler open while lag is over the SLO | | `RECENT_REPARENT` | info | a primary changed inside the window | ## Worked examples ### A drifted cluster Real output, captured from the bundled fixture: ```console $ .venv/bin/python -m vtmon check \ -d examples/desired-topology.yaml \ --fixture examples/drifted-snapshot.json --no-color vitess-topo-monitor declaration : [##############..............==============##############] -40 primary=zone1-100 replicas=3 rdonly=1 lag=3.2s scatter=4.1% 80-c0 primary=- replicas=3 rdonly=1 lag=9.5s scatter=6.6% c0- primary=zone2-400 replicas=2 rdonly=1 lag=5.5s scatter=27.7% customer (sharded) key space [############################============================] -80 primary=zone1-500 replicas=3 rdonly=0 lag=2.3s scatter=1.2% 80- primary=zone1-600 replicas=3 rdonly=0 lag=2.2s scatter=1.6% NOT-SERVING lookup (unsharded) key space [########################################################] - primary=zone1-700 replicas=1 rdonly=0 lag=0.7s FINDINGS [x] KEYRANGE_GAP commerce commerce: key range 40-80 is not served by any shard [x] SHARD_MISSING commerce/40-80 shard commerce/40-80 is declared but absent [x] NO_PRIMARY commerce/80-c0 shard commerce/80-c0 has no elected primary [x] KEYRANGE_GAP customer customer: key range 80- is not served by any shard [x] SHARD_NOT_SERVING customer/80- shard customer/80- has is_primary_serving=false [!] TABLET_COUNT_MISMATCH commerce/80-c0 shard commerce/80-c0 has 0 primary tablet(s) in zone1, expected 1 [!] PRIMARY_WRONG_CELL commerce/c0- shard commerce/c0- primary is in cell zone2 [!] SCATTER_RATIO_HIGH commerce/c0- scatter-query ratio for commerce/c0- is 27.7%, SLO is 20.0% [!] TABLET_COUNT_MISMATCH commerce/c0- shard commerce/c0- has 0 primary tablet(s) in FAIL 5 critical, 6 warning, 0 info $ echo $? 2 ``` The ASCII bar is the same coverage view the dashboard draws graphically: `#` and `=` alternate between adjacent shards, and `.` marks a span nothing is serving. The `commerce` bar visibly loses its second quarter. Here is that same state in the dashboard: ![The dashboard showing the degraded cluster: a hatched GAP segment in the commerce coverage bar, a shard card marked NO PRIMARY, and five critical alerts](docs/dashboard-drift.png) ### Replaying a multi-frame fixture `--replay-all` feeds every recorded frame through the reparent tracker before checking the last one, which is what surfaces failover history from a batch job: ```console $ .venv/bin/python -m vtmon check \ -d examples/desired-topology.yaml \ --fixture examples/cluster-snapshot.json --replay-all --no-color ... RECENT REPARENTS 2026-07-20 09:20:00Z commerce/80-c0: primary zone1-300 -> zone1-302 2026-07-16 07:30:00Z commerce/80-c0: primary none -> zone1-300 2026-07-13 16:30:00Z commerce/40-80: primary none -> zone1-200 FINDINGS [!] REPLICATION_LAG_HIGH commerce/40-80 zone1-201 is 93.1s behind, SLO is 30s [!] REPLICATION_LAG_HIGH commerce/40-80 zone1-203 is 83.8s behind, SLO is 30s [!] SCATTER_RATIO_HIGH commerce/c0- scatter-query ratio for commerce/c0- is 27.7%, SLO is 20.0% [!] TABLET_NOT_SERVING commerce/c0- zone1-403 (rdonly) is in state NOT_SERVING [i] THROTTLER_OPEN commerce/40-80 throttler is open on zone1-201 while lag is over SLO [i] THROTTLER_OPEN commerce/40-80 throttler is open on zone1-203 while lag is over SLO [i] RECENT_REPARENT commerce/80-c0 shard commerce/80-c0 reparented 11m ago to zone1-302 FAIL 0 critical, 4 warning, 3 info $ echo $? 1 ``` Note the pairing: the throttler being *open* while lag is over budget is a hint, not an alarm — it says VReplication or Online DDL work is being admitted and may be what is causing the lag. See [monitoring DDL lag during migrations](https://www.shardedtopology.org/observability-operations-for-sharded-vitess/monitoring-replication-lag-and-throttling/monitoring-ddl-lag-during-migrations/). ### Machine-readable output ```console $ .venv/bin/python -m vtmon alerts \ -d examples/desired-topology.yaml \ --fixture examples/drifted-snapshot.json \ --format json --min-severity critical [ { "code": "KEYRANGE_GAP", "severity": "critical", "keyspace": "commerce", "shard": null, "target": "commerce", "summary": "commerce: key range 40-80 is not served by any shard", "detail": "serving shards must partition the key space exactly once", "further_reading": "https://www.shardedtopology.org/vitess-sharding-architecture-topology-design/implementing-fallback-routing-for-shard-outages/", "labels": { "span": "40-80" } }, ... ] ``` ### The exported metrics ```console $ .venv/bin/python -m vtmon check -d examples/desired-topology.yaml \ --fixture examples/drifted-snapshot.json --metrics-out vtmon.prom $ grep -E '^vtmon_(up|findings_total|finding\{|keyrange)' vtmon.prom vtmon_up 1 vtmon_findings_total{severity="info"} 0 vtmon_findings_total{severity="warning"} 6 vtmon_findings_total{severity="critical"} 5 vtmon_finding{code="KEYRANGE_GAP",keyspace="commerce",severity="critical"} 1 vtmon_finding{code="SHARD_MISSING",keyspace="commerce",severity="critical",shard="40-80"} 1 vtmon_finding{code="NO_PRIMARY",keyspace="commerce",severity="critical",shard="80-c0"} 1 vtmon_finding{code="KEYRANGE_GAP",keyspace="customer",severity="critical"} 1 vtmon_finding{code="SHARD_NOT_SERVING",keyspace="customer",severity="critical",shard="80-"} 1 vtmon_finding{code="TABLET_COUNT_MISMATCH",keyspace="commerce",severity="warning",shard="80-c0"} 1 vtmon_finding{code="PRIMARY_WRONG_CELL",keyspace="commerce",severity="warning",shard="c0-"} 1 vtmon_finding{code="SCATTER_RATIO_HIGH",keyspace="commerce",severity="warning",shard="c0-"} 1 vtmon_finding{code="TABLET_COUNT_MISMATCH",keyspace="commerce",severity="warning",shard="c0-"} 2 vtmon_finding{code="TABLET_NOT_SERVING",keyspace="commerce",severity="warning",shard="c0-"} 1 vtmon_keyrange_coverage_ratio{keyspace="commerce"} 0.75 vtmon_keyrange_coverage_ratio{keyspace="customer"} 0.5 vtmon_keyrange_coverage_ratio{keyspace="lookup"} 1 ``` When `serve` is running, the same body is available at `/metrics` and is a valid Prometheus scrape target. ### Recording a fixture from a live cluster ```console $ .venv/bin/python -m vtmon snapshot \ --vtctld localhost:15999 \ --prometheus http://prometheus.internal:9090 \ -o snapshots/prod-$(date +%Y%m%dT%H%M).json wrote snapshots/prod-20260720T0930.json: 3 keyspace(s), 7 shard(s), 30 tablet(s) ``` Attach one of those to a bug report and anybody can reproduce your drift analysis offline. ## CLI reference ``` python -m vtmon [-v] [--version] COMMAND ... ``` | Global flag | Effect | | --- | --- | | `-v`, `--verbose` | more log detail; repeat for debug. In `check` it also prints finding details and deep links. | | `--version` | print the version and exit | ### Data-source flags (accepted by every subcommand) | Flag | Default | Description | | --- | --- | --- | | `--fixture PATH` | — | replay a recorded snapshot JSON file (offline) | | `--vtctld ADDR` | — | vtctld gRPC address, e.g. `localhost:15999`. Mutually exclusive with `--fixture`. | | `--vtctldclient BIN` | `vtctldclient` | path to the client binary | | `--prometheus URL` | — | Prometheus base URL used to enrich the snapshot | | `--promql-lag QUERY` | see above | override the replication-lag query | | `--promql-throttler QUERY` | see above | override the throttler query | | `--promql-scatter QUERY` | see above | override the scatter-query query | | `--promql-total QUERY` | see above | override the total-query query | | `--timeout SECONDS` | `30.0` | per-request timeout | ### `vtmon check` One-shot drift check. Exits non-zero when findings are present. | Flag | Default | Description | | --- | --- | --- | | `-d`, `--desired PATH` | *required* | the declaration YAML | | `--format {text,json}` | `text` | output format | | `--replay-all` | off | feed every frame of a multi-frame fixture through the reparent tracker first | | `--fail-on {info,warning,critical,never}` | `warning` | lowest severity that produces a non-zero exit | | `--no-color` | off | disable ANSI colour (also honours `NO_COLOR` / `FORCE_COLOR`) | | `--metrics-out PATH` | — | also write Prometheus text-format metrics to a file | ### `vtmon serve` Run the dashboard, the state API and `/metrics`. | Flag | Default | Description | | --- | --- | --- | | `-d`, `--desired PATH` | *required* | the declaration YAML | | `--host HOST` | `127.0.0.1` | bind address | | `--port PORT` | `8477` | bind port | | `--interval SECONDS` | `5.0` | collection interval | | `--alert-sink SPEC` | — | repeatable; `stdout`, `stdout:json`, `webhook:URL`, `slack:URL` | | `--alert-cooldown SECONDS` | `900` | per-finding alert cooldown | Routes: `/` (dashboard), `/api/state` (JSON the page polls), `/metrics` (Prometheus text), `/healthz` (503 while degraded), `/static/*`. ### `vtmon snapshot` Record a cluster to a fixture JSON file. | Flag | Default | Description | | --- | --- | --- | | `-o`, `--output PATH` | *required* | file to write | | `--keyspace NAME` | all | repeatable; restrict to these keyspaces | ### `vtmon alerts` Render, and optionally dispatch, the current alerts. | Flag | Default | Description | | --- | --- | --- | | `-d`, `--desired PATH` | *required* | the declaration YAML | | `--format {text,json}` | `text` | output format | | `--min-severity {info,warning,critical}` | `warning` | lowest severity to report | | `--sink SPEC` | — | repeatable; dispatch to `stdout`, `webhook:URL`, `slack:URL` | | `--no-color` | off | disable ANSI colour | ## Alerting Sinks are pluggable and all three ship in the box: - **`stdout`** — one line per finding; `stdout:json` emits a single JSON document instead. - **`webhook:URL`** — a generic `POST` carrying `{source, generated_at, context, count, worst_severity, findings[]}`. - **`slack:URL`** — a Slack incoming-webhook document with `blocks`, including the further-reading link on every finding. In front of the sinks sits a router that applies dedupe and cooldown, so a shard that flaps every fifteen seconds does not produce an alert every fifteen seconds: - a finding is identified by `code:keyspace/shard`; - the first sighting fires immediately; - it will not fire again until the cooldown elapses — **unless its severity increased**, which always fires; - once a finding stops appearing for two consecutive cycles it is marked resolved and may fire immediately if it returns. One failing sink does not stop the others; failures are collected and raised together after every sink has been attempted. ## Grafana and Prometheus `contrib/` holds two ready-to-use artefacts, both written against exactly the series this tool exports: - **`contrib/grafana-dashboard.json`** — import it and pick your Prometheus datasource. Panels: monitor health, findings by severity over time, a filterable table of active findings, replication lag / healthy replicas / scatter ratio / reparents per shard, and key-range coverage per keyspace. - **`contrib/prometheus-rules.yml`** — recording rules plus alerting rules for every critical finding code, with runbook links into the field guide. Scrape the dashboard like any other target: ```yaml scrape_configs: - job_name: vtmon static_configs: - targets: ['vtmon.internal:8477'] ``` For the wider dashboard-building picture, see [building a VTGate latency dashboard](https://www.shardedtopology.org/observability-operations-for-sharded-vitess/monitoring-vtgate-query-latency/building-a-vtgate-latency-dashboard/). ## Configuration There are no config files beyond the declaration; everything else is flags. Two environment variables are honoured: | Variable | Effect | | --- | --- | | `NO_COLOR` | disable ANSI colour in terminal output | | `FORCE_COLOR` | force ANSI colour even when stdout is not a TTY | The dashboard also accepts `?theme=light` or `?theme=dark` to pin the colour theme (otherwise it follows the browser and remembers the toggle in `localStorage`). ## Exit codes | Code | Meaning | | --- | --- | | `0` | no findings at or above `--fail-on` | | `1` | worst finding is a warning | | `2` | at least one critical finding | | `3` | usage or declaration error | | `4` | the collector failed (bad fixture, unreachable vtctld, missing binary) | Cron-friendly: ```cron # Fail the job (and mail the operator) whenever the cluster drifts. */5 * * * * cd /opt/vitess-topo-monitor && .venv/bin/python -m vtmon check \ -d /etc/vtmon/topology.yaml --vtctld localhost:15999 \ --prometheus http://prom:9090 --no-color # Or push straight to Slack, only for critical drift. */5 * * * * cd /opt/vitess-topo-monitor && .venv/bin/python -m vtmon alerts \ -d /etc/vtmon/topology.yaml --vtctld localhost:15999 \ --min-severity critical --sink "slack:$SLACK_URL" ``` ## Limitations Being honest about what this does not do: - **No VSchema analysis.** The tool reasons about shards, tablets and key ranges. It does not read your VSchema, so it cannot tell you that a table is missing a primary vindex — only that the resulting scatter ratio is above your SLO. Diagnosing *why* a query scatters is a separate job. - **Metric names are version-sensitive.** The defaults target Vitess v20/v21. On other versions you will need the `--promql-*` overrides. The tool cannot detect your Vitess version. - **Throttler state is inferred, not read.** `THROTTLER_OPEN` / `THROTTLER_CLOSED` are derived from whether the throttler's check counter is advancing, which is a proxy for "the throttler is admitting work". It is not the same as querying the throttler's own status endpoint, and it is per-shard rather than per-check-name. - **Reparent history is only as deep as your snapshots.** Running `check` from cron sees one snapshot per invocation, so it detects reparents via `primary_term_start_time` but cannot reconstruct a timeline it never observed. `serve` keeps seven days of events in memory — **in memory**, so a restart loses the timeline. There is no persistent event store. - **`vtctldclient` is invoked as a subprocess.** That inherits its authentication, which is convenient, but means one process spawn per call and no connection reuse. It is fine at a five-second poll interval; it is not a high-frequency API. - **Single-cluster.** One declaration describes one topology server. Watching several clusters means running several instances. - **No historical storage.** `/metrics` is a snapshot of *now*. Trends live in your Prometheus, not here. - **Key-range fractions are approximate.** The coverage bar and gap sizes use the first four bytes of each boundary, which is ample for display but is not exact for pathologically deep boundaries. ## Development ```bash .venv/bin/python -m pytest # 229 tests, all offline .venv/bin/ruff check . ``` CI runs both on Python 3.11, 3.12 and 3.13. The layout separates concerns deliberately: ``` vtmon/ keyrange.py key-range arithmetic and coverage analysis models.py dataclasses for desired and observed topology desired.py declaration parsing and validation snapshotio.py snapshot JSON serialisation collectors/ fixture, vtctldclient and Prometheus collectors events.py reparent detection, timeline, flap detection drift.py the analysis engine (pure: inputs in, findings out) metrics.py Prometheus text exposition alerting.py sinks plus the dedupe/cooldown router render.py terminal rendering links.py further-reading deep links per finding code web/ aiohttp app, state projection, hand-written static assets cli.py argparse front end ``` The drift engine is a pure function of `(declaration, snapshot, events)`, which is why the test suite can provoke all twenty finding codes without a cluster. ## Further reading This tool was built alongside the Sharded Topology field guide, and the finding deep links point back into it. The pages most relevant to what the tool measures: - [Observability and operations for sharded Vitess](https://www.shardedtopology.org/observability-operations-for-sharded-vitess/) — the umbrella chapter. - [Monitoring replication lag and throttling](https://www.shardedtopology.org/observability-operations-for-sharded-vitess/monitoring-replication-lag-and-throttling/) — what `REPLICATION_LAG_HIGH` and the throttler findings are really telling you. - [Key VTTablet Prometheus metrics to watch](https://www.shardedtopology.org/observability-operations-for-sharded-vitess/monitoring-replication-lag-and-throttling/key-vttablet-prometheus-metrics-to-watch/) — the metric names behind the default PromQL. - [Monitoring DDL lag during migrations](https://www.shardedtopology.org/observability-operations-for-sharded-vitess/monitoring-replication-lag-and-throttling/monitoring-ddl-lag-during-migrations/) — why an open throttler and high lag often travel together. - [Monitoring VTGate query latency](https://www.shardedtopology.org/observability-operations-for-sharded-vitess/monitoring-vtgate-query-latency/) and [building a VTGate latency dashboard](https://www.shardedtopology.org/observability-operations-for-sharded-vitess/monitoring-vtgate-query-latency/building-a-vtgate-latency-dashboard/). - [Alerting on scatter-query ratio](https://www.shardedtopology.org/observability-operations-for-sharded-vitess/monitoring-vtgate-query-latency/alerting-on-scatter-query-ratio/) — the background for `SCATTER_RATIO_HIGH` and for picking a sane SLO. - [Configuring VTTablet for high availability](https://www.shardedtopology.org/vitess-sharding-architecture-topology-design/designing-horizontal-shard-topologies/configuring-vttablet-for-high-availability/) — replica counts, promotion candidates and why `REPLICA_COUNT_LOW` is critical rather than a warning. - [Implementing fallback routing for shard outages](https://www.shardedtopology.org/vitess-sharding-architecture-topology-design/implementing-fallback-routing-for-shard-outages/) — what actually happens to a query that hits a key-range gap. - [Circuit breaking for degraded shards](https://www.shardedtopology.org/vitess-sharding-architecture-topology-design/implementing-fallback-routing-for-shard-outages/circuit-breaking-for-degraded-shards/) — what to do about a shard that is serving but sick. ## Licence MIT — see [LICENSE](LICENSE).

documents.plain_text: # Auto-Certificate-Renewal File Name : ssl_renew_all_sites.sh #!/bin/bash export PATH=$PATH:/usr/local/bin LOG_DIR="/home/user_name/crons_file" LOG_FILE="$LOG_DIR/ssl-renew-cron.log" DATE=$(date '+%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S') echo "SSL renewal started at $DATE" >> "$LOG_FILE" echo "Stopping nginx..." >> "$LOG_FILE" sudo systemctl stop nginx >> "$LOG_FILE" 2>&1 echo "Running certbot renew..." >> "$LOG_FILE" sudo /usr/local/bin/certbot renew >> "$LOG_FILE" 2>&1 echo "Starting nginx..." >> "$LOG_FILE" sudo systemctl start nginx >> "$LOG_FILE" 2>&1 DATE_END=$(date '+%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S') echo "SSL renewal completed at $DATE_END" >> "$LOG_FILE" echo "-------------------------------------------" >> "$LOG_FILE" Cron : ( sudo crontab -e ) Add Below Line in crontab 0 6 * * 1 /home/user_name/crons_file/ssl_renew_all_sites.sh >> /home/user_name/crons_file/cron_output.log 2>&1

documents.plain_text: # PCB Designer AI Agent End-to-End PCB Design Assistant powered by LLMs. This is a **universal** AI hardware agent built in Python. It supports any major LLM provider (Claude, Gemini, OpenAI) as well as local models (Ollama, LM Studio) to autonomously generate schematics and PCB layouts from natural language. *Note: We have also tested and ported this agent as a seamless, browser-based hardware design environment for **Anna OS**! (See deployment section below).* ## How it works The agent takes a natural-language description (e.g., "Design a board with an ESP32, an IMU sensor, a LiPo battery charger, a USB-C port, a 3.3V LDO, and an SD card slot"), and automatically: 1. Parses the requirements using an LLM. 2. Maps keywords to real physical components (BOM generation). 3. Synthesizes a schematic netlist. 4. Generates standard IPC footprint geometries (SOIC, LQFP, SOT-223, USB-C, etc.). 5. Renders a complete, routing-ready `.kicad_pcb` board file! ## Getting Started (Universal Usage) The agent runs as a standalone JSON-RPC service. You can pipe a prompt directly to it. ### 1. Configure your LLM Provider The agent is model-agnostic. You must set environment variables to tell the agent which API to use. **To use Anthropic (Claude):** ```bash export PCB_AI_LLM_PROVIDER=claude export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=your_api_key_here export PCB_AI_MODEL=claude-3-5-sonnet-20240620 ``` **To use Gemini:** ```bash export PCB_AI_LLM_PROVIDER=gemini export GEMINI_API_KEY=your_api_key_here export PCB_AI_MODEL=gemini-3.6-flash ``` **To use OpenRouter (Auto-Fallback across Free Models):** ```bash export PCB_AI_LLM_PROVIDER=openrouter export OPENROUTER_API_KEY=your_api_key_here # The agent will automatically fallback through a robust list of free models # (e.g. dots-3-note-preview, qwen3.8-27b) if rate-limits are hit! ``` **To use OpenAI:** ```bash export PCB_AI_LLM_PROVIDER=openai export OPENAI_API_KEY=your_api_key_here export PCB_AI_MODEL=gpt-4o-mini ``` **To use Local Models (LM Studio / Ollama):** ```bash export PCB_AI_LLM_PROVIDER=lmstudio # or ollama # Ensure your local server is running on port 1234 (LM Studio) or 11434 (Ollama) ``` > 💡 **Hardware Recommendation (16GB VRAM GPUs):** If you are running local models on a GPU with 16GB of VRAM, we strongly recommend using the **`google/gemma-4-12b`** model. In our internal benchmark testing, Gemma correctly identified standard EE footprints, parsed mechanical datasheets, and reliably output strictly formatted JSON data, whereas models like Qwen or Bonsai often hallucinated physical package geometries and failed data extraction tasks. ### 2. Run the Agent Locally You can interact with the agent using the provided `test_rpc.py` script, which sends a test prompt to the pipeline: ```bash python3 test_rpc.py ``` This will execute the agent pipeline end-to-end and output the generated BOM, Netlist, and Board files in JSON format! ## Anna OS Integration While the agent is completely universal, it can also be deployed seamlessly to the Anna OS App Store. ```bash cd anna-app anna-app dev ``` This spins up a local UI at `http://localhost:5173`. When deployed this way, if no API keys are provided, it can gracefully fallback to using Anna OS quota/tokens. ## Running the Reef Evaluation Harness We include a local testing harness powered by [Reef](https://github.com/reef-ai) to evaluate how well different LLMs extract footprint package parameters from PDF datasheets. ```bash cd reef_harness reef serve -c serve.yaml ``` ## Contributing PRs welcome. Priority areas: - Datasheet parsers and CV feature extractors - SKiDL schematic reference circuit templates - Freerouting DSN/SES integration ## License Dual-licensed: - Non-commercial, open-source use granted under the Custom License in `LICENSE`. - Commercial/enterprise use requires prior written authorisation from the author. Contact: assalas@tutamail.com.

The application allows users to: * Log shipment temperature data * Detect temperature violations automatically * Monitor shipment conditions in real time * View logs in a live dashboard * Store and retrieve shipment data using MongoDB --- # 🚀 Features ✅ Shipment temperature logging ✅ Real-time monitoring dashboard ✅ Automatic status detection: * Normal * Warning * Critical ✅ MongoDB database integration ✅ REST API support ✅ Responsive UI design ✅ Auto-refresh dashboard ✅ Temperature analytics and statistics --- # 🛠 Tech Stack ## Frontend * HTML5 * CSS3 * JavaScript ## Backend * Node.js * Express.js ## Database * MongoDB * Mongoose ## Tools * Nodemon * Postman * MongoDB Compass --- # 📂 Project Structure ```bash cold-chain-monitoring/ │ ├── public/ │ ├── index.html │ └── dashboard.html │ ├── index.js ├── package.json ├── .env └── README.md ``` --- # ⚙️ Installation & Setup ## 1️⃣ Clone Repository ```bash git clone https://github.com/your-username/cold-chain-monitoring.git cd cold-chain-monitoring ``` --- ## 2️⃣ Install Dependencies ```bash npm install ``` --- ## 3️⃣ Configure Environment Variables Create a `.env` file: ```env MONGODB_URI=mongodb://127.0.0.1:27017/cold-chain-monitoring PORT=3000 ``` --- ## 4️⃣ Start MongoDB ```bash net start MongoDB ``` --- ## 5️⃣ Run Project ### Production ```bash npm start ``` ### Development ```bash npm run dev ``` --- # 🌐 Application URLs ## Log Entry Page ```bash http://localhost:3000/ ``` ## Dashboard ```bash http://localhost:3000/dashboard ``` --- # 📡 API Endpoints ## POST `/log` Save shipment temperature log. ### Request Body ```json { "shipment_id": "SHIP001", "location": "Pune", "temperature": 5 } ``` --- ## GET `/logs` Retrieve all shipment logs. --- ## GET `/logs/:shipment_id` Retrieve logs for a specific shipment. --- ## GET `/health` Check backend server health. --- # 🧠 Status Detection Logic | Temperature Range | Status | | ---------------------- | -------- | | 4°C - 6°C | Normal | | 2°C - 4°C or 6°C - 8°C | Warning | | Below 2°C or Above 8°C | Critical | --- # 📊 Dashboard Features * Real-time shipment monitoring * Auto-refresh every 10 seconds * Shipment statistics * Color-coded status indicators * Temperature tracking table --- # 🗃 Database Schema ```js { shipment_id: String, location: String, temperature: Number, status: String, timestamp: Date } ``` --- # 🧪 Testing You can test APIs using: * Postman * Browser * MongoDB Compass --- # 📸 Screenshots ## Log Entry Page (Add screenshot here) ## Dashboard (Add screenshot here) --- # 👨‍💻 Team Members | Name | Role | | --------------- | ---------------------------- | | Arya Pradeep | Product Owner / DB Developer | | Ayush Joshi | Scrum Master / DB Developer | | Rushabh Kamdi | DB Architect / DB Developer | | Atharv Jambhule | App Developer / DB Developer | --- # 🎯 Future Enhancements * IoT sensor integration * GPS tracking * Email/SMS alerts * Cloud deployment * Data analytics * AI-based prediction system --- # 📜 License This project is developed for academic and educational purposes.

documents.plain_text: # Nature and Biodiversity Investment Agent > **Responsible AI:** Analyst-controlled research; verify evidence, disclose AI assistance and protect confidential information. [Policy and project-specific checks](RESPONSIBLE_AI.md). **New research, 21 October 2026:** [Brazil agriculture — who captures productivity, and what happens to land?](examples/brazil-agriculture/README.md) An original decomposition of CONAB's first 2026/27 survey separates output, crop area and yield; a transparent farm scenario tests price/cost capture and the limits of land-sparing claims. [Chart and memo](examples/brazil-agriculture/README.md) · [Runnable results](examples/brazil-agriculture/RESULTS.md). Public evidence plus labelled scenarios; issuer and nature attribution remain `NEEDS_DATA`. [![Validate research workflow](https://github.com/HHFinAi/Nature-and-Biodiversity-Investment-Agent/actions/workflows/validate.yml/badge.svg?branch=main)](https://github.com/HHFinAi/Nature-and-Biodiversity-Investment-Agent/actions/workflows/validate.yml) **Institutional-quality buy-side research, designed to support tradable investment decisions through a traceable, auditable workflow.** Connects location-specific ecosystem dependencies, measured outcomes, rights and financial transmission without inventing a universal biodiversity score or assuming tradability. Built by **HHFinAi** for investment analysts, fixed-income/equity specialists, portfolio managers and investment committees. Start with the [integrated portfolio research handoff](examples/integrated-portfolio/README.md): a public-data model portfolio connects carbon attribution to named water/location questions and financial evidence gates. Site dependencies and issuer financial effects remain distinct; proposed questions do not establish measured nature outcomes. **Institutional quality describes the designed process controls—not independent audit certification, production readiness, client adoption or guaranteed investment accuracy.** “Tradable” requires a verified investment instrument and appropriate market, legal and portfolio evidence; many private projects and programmes are not liquid or investable. “Auditable” means inspectable local records, not authenticated or tamper-proof recordkeeping. No trade execution is provided. Version **0.1.0** · **14 specialist stages** · **5 routes** · Python **3.10+ target** · **Human review** [Workflow](WORKFLOW.md) · [Prompts and skills](PROMPTS.md) · [Evidence trail](docs/AUDIT.md) · [Institutional-quality controls](docs/INSTITUTIONAL_QUALITY.md) · [Validation](docs/VALIDATION.md) · [FAQ](docs/FAQ.md) The [AI infrastructure handoff](examples/ai-infrastructure/README.md), prepared 16 October 2026, defines location-level water and land evidence gates linked to a financial model. Site dependencies, measured outcomes and project costs remain distinct. ## What does this buy-side agent do? Nature-related investment risk, biodiversity outcomes and project underwriting. The local engine freezes the research request, prompts and methodology register; emits host work packets; validates structured evidence, units and calculations; enforces stage dependencies; archives superseded findings; invalidates downstream decisions; and records explicit human research review. It exports a committee packet, claim ledger, evidence ledger and complete JSON lineage. The host AI or human performs the actual research through separately authorized tools. **No embedded LLM, live data feed, automatic source extraction, scheduler or broker connection is included.** Synthetic demonstrations test workflow mechanics; they do not run live investment analysis. The incomplete primary-source study demonstrates safe stopping, not completed diligence. ## Choose a research route | Route | Stages | Asset types | |---|---:|---| | `listed-equity` | 14 | equity | | `public-credit` | 14 | bond | | `private-nature-project` | 14 | private_project | | `portfolio-screen` | 14 | equity, bond, portfolio | | `nature-credit` | 14 | biodiversity_credit, private_project | ## Run the tested local workflow From this repository's root, with Python 3.10 or later: ```bash python3 -m unittest discover -s tests -v python3 scripts/check_repository.py python3 -m sf_agent routes python3 -m sf_agent demo --out runs/demo-01 python3 -m sf_agent report --run runs/demo-01 python3 -m sf_agent export --run runs/demo-01 --out exports/demo-01 python3 -m sf_agent source-study --out runs/source-study-01 ``` No third-party runtime packages, credentials or network access are required for these commands. Use a fresh output directory each time. The `source-study` command deliberately returns a NEEDS_DATA research status because material evidence is absent; that is the intended control demonstration, not an analysis to trade on. Process exit 0 means the command ran, not that the investment research is approved. ## Inspect actual example outputs [Synthetic packet](examples/reports/synthetic-packet.md) · [Incomplete historical source study](examples/reports/source-study-packet.md) · [Calculation input](examples/calculation-arguments.json) ```bash python3 -m sf_agent calc --operation nature_cashflow_stress --arguments examples/calculation-arguments.json --currency USD ``` The calculation is illustrative and uses explicit assumptions. See [methodology and operation boundaries](docs/METHODOLOGY.md). The test suite is not evidence of investment alpha, impact causality, regulatory compliance or current trade suitability. ## Use the prompts for real research Start with `examples/research-request-template.json`, replace every placeholder, identify actual instruments, register reviewed permitted evidence and set explicit freshness policies. Follow the [host workflow](WORKFLOW.md) and [artifact guide](templates/host-artifact-guide.md). `next` emits the stage contract and upstream evidence context; submit actual research artifacts using the latest revision. Do not use deterministic fixtures to complete a research run. Use the complete folder with `SKILL.md` in a filesystem-enabled agent host. Child skills are under `skills/`. Host installation/activation is not certified, and copying a prompt into a text-only chat does not enforce the Python state machine. Do not call the human approval command from an autonomous host agent. ## What makes the evidence layer auditable? Every numerical source claim binds to its evidence metric and original unit. Every allowlisted calculation declares input provenance and is recomputed. The run freezes adopted instructions and input metadata; revisions archive affected outputs and revoke prior review. Unknown data remains unknown, open material issues block approval, and synthetic/source-study modes cannot be research-approved. See the [claim-to-control matrix](docs/INSTITUTIONAL_QUALITY.md) for enforced versus procedural controls and missing capabilities. ## Published repository and local synchronization The source code is published at [HHFinAi/Nature-and-Biodiversity-Investment-Agent](https://github.com/HHFinAi/Nature-and-Biodiversity-Investment-Agent). In GitHub Desktop, use **Fetch origin** and **Pull origin** before editing an existing clone. Preserve its `.git` directory and review changes on a working branch. The [Desktop guide](START_HERE_GITHUB_DESKTOP.md) covers synchronization and initial publication of a separate new copy. `repository-metadata.json` records this repository's identity, About description and topics. [GEO/search documentation](docs/GEO_SEO.md) uses visible content, citations and clear structure; it does not promise search rankings or AI citations. ## Licence, sources and limitations Original code, prompts and examples: MIT, Copyright 2026 HHFinAi. See [NOTICE](NOTICE.md) for upstream lineage and third-party rights. No affiliation with or endorsement by referenced standard setters or institutions. Read [method sources](references/SOURCES.md), [data requirements](docs/DATA_SOURCES.md), [security](SECURITY.md), [FAQ](docs/FAQ.md) and the actual [validation record](docs/VALIDATION.md) before use.

documents.plain_text: # 🩺 Population Health Risk Trend Analysis > End-to-end SQL + Python + Power BI pipeline that identifies high-risk patient > segments across a **10,000-patient** cohort, enabling care managers to > prioritize outreach and intervention planning. ![Python](https://img.shields.io/badge/python-Pandas%20%7C%20NumPy-green) ![SQL](https://img.shields.io/badge/SQL-DuckDB-blue) ![Power BI](https://img.shields.io/badge/Power%20BI-dashboard-yellow) ![License](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-MIT-lightgrey) --- ## Overview Population health programs live or die on three questions: **who is at risk**, **which care gaps are open**, and **how demand is trending**. This project answers all three with a reproducible pipeline that turns raw EHR-style extracts into risk tiers, care-gap worklists, screening-compliance KPIs, and a five-page Power BI dashboard. **Coverage:** - **Preventive care** — flu vaccination, mammogram, colonoscopy, and annual wellness visit compliance against eligibility-based (HEDIS-style) denominators - **Chronic-condition monitoring** — A1c testing & control for diabetics, blood pressure control for hypertensives, LDL testing, KDIGO-style CKD staging - **Screening compliance & care gaps** — seven engineered care-gap flags rolled into per-patient gap counts and a prioritized outreach worklist > **Privacy note:** all data is fully synthetic, generated locally by > `src/generate_ehr_data.py`. No real patient information is used anywhere. --- ## Architecture — where each tool does its job ``` ┌─────────────────────────────┐ │ generate_ehr_data.py │ PYTHON — synthetic EHR extracts: │ │ patients · conditions · encounters · │ │ labs · screenings (→ Parquet) └──────────────┬──────────────┘ ┌──────────────▼──────────────┐ │ prepare_indicators.py │ PYTHON (Pandas/NumPy) — the data-prep │ │ workflows: screening compliance, chronic │ │ control, care-gap engineering, risk │ │ scoring → patient_indicators spine └──────────────┬──────────────┘ ┌──────────────▼──────────────┐ │ DuckDB warehouse │ SQL — 6 analyses: risk segments, gap │ + sql/01..06 │ prevalence, screening compliance, │ │ chronic control, utilization trends, │ │ outreach worklist └──────────────┬──────────────┘ ┌──────────────▼──────────────┐ │ export_powerbi_dataset.py │ → star schema CSVs (4 facts + 2 dims) └──────────────┬──────────────┘ ┌──────────────▼──────────────┐ │ POWER BI │ 5-page dashboard: exec overview, │ powerbi/ │ screening compliance, chronic control, │ │ utilization trends, outreach worklist └─────────────────────────────┘ ``` Division of labor is deliberate: **Python** handles data preparation and feature/indicator engineering (where row-wise clinical logic lives naturally), **SQL** handles set-based population analytics (readable, portable, warehouse-ready), and **Power BI** handles the interactive layer care managers actually use. --- ## Dataset at a glance (default run: `--patients 10000 --seed 42`) | Extract | Rows | Description | |---|---:|---| | patients | 10,000 | Demographics, payer, PCP assignment | | conditions | 5,854 | Chronic diagnoses (8 conditions, ICD-10) | | encounters | 67,111 | Visits across 5 encounter types, 2023–2025 | | labs | 12,234 | HbA1c, systolic BP, LDL, eGFR results | | screenings | 27,862 | Flu, mammogram, colonoscopy, wellness visits | | **patient_indicators** | **10,000 × 48** | **Python-engineered analytics spine** | --- ## Quickstart ```bash make install # pip install -r requirements.txt make all # data → prep → build → analyze → powerbi ``` Individual stages: `make data` · `make prep` · `make build` · `make analyze` · `make powerbi`. Scale up with `make all PATIENTS=50000`. Then open Power BI Desktop and follow [`powerbi/DASHBOARD_GUIDE.md`](powerbi/DASHBOARD_GUIDE.md) (~30 min) using the exported dataset in `powerbi/dataset/` and the measures in [`powerbi/DAX_MEASURES.md`](powerbi/DAX_MEASURES.md). --- ## Key results (default run) ### Risk stratification (`sql/01_risk_segments.sql`) | Tier | Patients | % of pop | Avg age | Avg chronic | Avg open gaps | Avg ED visits | |---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:| | Critical | 78 | 0.8% | 72.8 | 3.01 | 2.44 | 2.14 | | High | 714 | 7.1% | 67.8 | 2.03 | 1.59 | 1.38 | | Moderate | 2,464 | 24.6% | 61.3 | 1.11 | 1.16 | 0.86 | | Low | 6,744 | 67.4% | 46.6 | 0.21 | 0.55 | 0.30 | **~8% of the population (High + Critical) carries 3–15× the chronic burden and ED utilization of the Low tier** — the outreach panel worth prioritizing. ### Care-gap targeting (`sql/02_care_gap_prevalence.sql`) The clinical-control gaps concentrate sharply in high-risk tiers — **67.6% of uncontrolled-A1c gaps and 55.1% of overdue-A1c gaps sit in High/Critical patients** — validating that the risk model surfaces actionable clinical need, not just volume. Population-wide screening gaps (colonoscopy due: 24.6%, no PCP: 18.1%) are broader but shallower. ### Screening compliance (`sql/03_screening_compliance.sql`) | Measure | Eligible | Compliance | |---|---:|---:| | Flu vaccine (2025 season) | 10,000 | 55.3% | | Colonoscopy (ages 45–75) | 5,854 | 58.1% | | A1c test in 12mo (diabetics) | 733 | 60.2% | | Mammogram (F 50–74) | 2,453 | 61.6% | | Annual wellness visit | 10,000 | 64.1% | ### Chronic control (`sql/04_chronic_control.sql`) A1c control ( < 8.0) among diabetics: **53.8%** · BP control ( < 140) among hypertensives: **53.1%** — both leave a large improvement runway that the outreach worklist (`sql/06`) turns into a ranked, gap-annotated call list. --- ## Power BI dashboard Five pages, specified visual-by-visual in the build guide: 1. **Executive Overview** — population KPIs, risk-tier donut, gaps by tier 2. **Screening Compliance** — HEDIS-style rates vs. 70% target, payer equity matrix 3. **Chronic Condition Control** — A1c/BP control, A1c distribution, CKD staging 4. **Utilization Trends** — monthly encounters + 3-mo average, ED trend, YoY 5. **Outreach Worklist** — ranked High/Critical patients with conditional formatting and a care-gap slicer The `powerbi/` folder ships the star-schema dataset (4 fact + 2 dimension tables), 25+ DAX measures, a custom theme, and the step-by-step guide. Build the `.pbix` in Power BI Desktop and commit it alongside. --- ## Project structure ``` population-health-risk-trends/ ├── README.md · LICENSE · Makefile · requirements.txt ├── sql/ │ ├── 00_schema.sql care-gap & calendar views │ ├── 01_risk_segments.sql │ ├── 02_care_gap_prevalence.sql │ ├── 03_screening_compliance.sql │ ├── 04_chronic_control.sql │ ├── 05_utilization_trends.sql │ └── 06_outreach_worklist.sql ├── src/ │ ├── generate_ehr_data.py synthetic EHR extracts │ ├── prepare_indicators.py Pandas/NumPy indicator pipeline │ ├── build_database.py Parquet → DuckDB + schema │ ├── run_analysis.py SQL runner → CSV + summary.md │ └── export_powerbi_dataset.py star-schema export for Power BI ├── powerbi/ │ ├── dataset/ committed CSVs (BI handoff) │ ├── DAX_MEASURES.md 25+ measures, grouped by page │ ├── DASHBOARD_GUIDE.md visual-by-visual build steps │ └── theme.json custom report theme ├── data/ · outputs/ generated (git-ignored) └── docs/ ``` --- ## Design notes - **Eligibility-based denominators.** Compliance rates only count eligible patients (e.g., mammogram: women 50–74), mirroring HEDIS measure discipline. - **Transparent risk model.** The score weights chronic burden, ED reliance, open gaps, age, CKD severity, and uncontrolled A1c — every point is explainable to a clinician, and the structure accepts an HCC/ML swap later. - **Committed BI dataset.** `powerbi/dataset/` is versioned on purpose: it's the contract between the data pipeline and the dashboard, so the report is buildable without running Python. - **Reproducible.** Fixed seed → identical data and results on every run. --- ## Tech stack **Python** (Pandas, NumPy, PyArrow) · **SQL** (DuckDB — window functions, CTEs, `STRING_AGG`, portable to Snowflake/Postgres) · **Power BI** (star schema, DAX, custom theme) · **Parquet** · **Make** ## License MIT — see [LICENSE](LICENSE).

documents.plain_text: # TrackAid TrackAid is a public accountability platform for Philippine disaster-relief fundraising. It connects verified campaigns, PayMongo-hosted payments, evidence review, public reconciliation, and signed Solana ledger records. **Production:** [trackaid.vercel.app](https://trackaid.vercel.app) **Repository:** [github.com/Josh112406/trackaid](https://github.com/Josh112406/trackaid) ## What TrackAid does - Lets organizations and community members submit fundraising programs with public proof. - Requires organization verification before a campaign can accept donations. - Sends donors to PayMongo Checkout, so TrackAid never receives card or wallet credentials. - Reconciles every confirmed donation into gross PHP amount, PayMongo fee, and net recipient amount. - Supports PayMongo Split Payments for approved organization merchant accounts. - Publishes campaign totals, disbursements, evidence fingerprints, and public ledger links. - Writes exact PHP-centavo accounting records and SHA-256 fingerprints to Solana Devnet. - Provides authenticated administration, analytics, CSV reports, audit logs, and payout routing. TrackAid does **not** create a token or convert PHP to cryptocurrency. One peso paid remains one peso in the PayMongo settlement flow. The Solana memo is a signed accounting representation only; it cannot receive, hold, or transfer the donation. ## System flow ```text Program submission │ ▼ Evidence and organization review ──► payout verification │ ▼ Published campaign │ ▼ PayMongo Checkout ──► PHP settlement to approved recipient │ ▼ Signed webhook reconciliation │ ├──► Supabase: gross, fee, net, audit entry, analytics │ └──► Solana Devnet: record ID, PHP centavos, SHA-256 fingerprint ``` The browser redirect is never treated as payment proof. A donation becomes paid only after the server verifies a PayMongo event and matches its campaign, checkout, donation, environment, and amount. ## Technology | Layer | Technology | | --------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------- | | Web application | Next.js 16 App Router, React 19, TypeScript | | Database, authentication, storage | Supabase Postgres, Auth, Storage, Row Level Security | | Payments | PayMongo Checkout API v2 and signed webhooks | | Public integrity ledger | Solana Kit and the public Memo program on Devnet | | Hosting | Vercel | | Tests | Vitest and Playwright | ## Project structure ```text app/ Next.js pages, admin views, and route handlers components/ Shared public and administrative UI lib/ Payments, reconciliation, Supabase, CSV, and ledger logic scripts/ Browser and operational verification supabase/migrations/ Database schema, policies, triggers, and security controls supabase/functions/ Official-source monitoring function vercel.json Scheduled ledger processing ``` ## Local setup Requirements: Node.js 22+, pnpm 11, Supabase, PayMongo, and Vercel projects. 1. Install dependencies. ```bash git clone https://github.com/Josh112406/trackaid.git cd trackaid pnpm install ``` 2. Create `.env.local`. Never commit this file. ```dotenv NEXT_PUBLIC_SITE_URL=http://localhost:3000 NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL=https://YOUR_PROJECT.supabase.co NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_PUBLISHABLE_KEY=YOUR_PUBLISHABLE_KEY SUPABASE_SECRET_KEY=YOUR_SERVER_SECRET_KEY PAYMONGO_SECRET_KEY=YOUR_SECRET_KEY PAYMONGO_WEBHOOK_SECRET=YOUR_WEBHOOK_SECRET PAYMONGO_LIVE_MODE=false SOLANA_DEVNET_RPC_URL=https://api.devnet.solana.com SOLANA_LEDGER_SIGNER_ADDRESS=YOUR_PUBLIC_SOLANA_ADDRESS SOLANA_LEDGER_SECRET_KEY=YOUR_BASE64_64_BYTE_SECRET CRON_SECRET=USE_A_LONG_RANDOM_VALUE ``` 3. Link Supabase and apply the migrations. ```bash pnpm exec supabase login pnpm exec supabase link --project-ref YOUR_PROJECT_REF pnpm exec supabase db push ``` 4. Run the app. ```bash pnpm dev ``` ## Environment variables | Variable | Scope | Purpose | | -------------------------------------- | ------------ | ------------------------------------------ | | `NEXT_PUBLIC_SITE_URL` | Public | Stable origin used in PayMongo return URLs | | `NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL` | Public | Supabase project API URL | | `NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_PUBLISHABLE_KEY` | Public | Browser-safe key protected by RLS | | `SUPABASE_SECRET_KEY` | Server only | Trusted database administration | | `PAYMONGO_SECRET_KEY` | Server only | PayMongo API authentication | | `PAYMONGO_WEBHOOK_SECRET` | Server only | Verifies the `Paymongo-Signature` header | | `PAYMONGO_LIVE_MODE` | Server only | Must match the configured PayMongo keys | | `SOLANA_DEVNET_RPC_URL` | Server only | Solana Devnet JSON-RPC endpoint | | `SOLANA_LEDGER_SIGNER_ADDRESS` | Public value | Dedicated ledger recorder address | | `SOLANA_LEDGER_SECRET_KEY` | Server only | Base64-encoded 64-byte signing key | | `SECURITY_HASH_PEPPER` | Server only | Optional dedicated rate-limit HMAC key | | `CRON_SECRET` | Server only | Authorizes the scheduled ledger worker | Never prefix secrets with `NEXT_PUBLIC_`. The Supabase Edge Function uses the platform-provided `SUPABASE_URL` and `SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY`. ## Supabase and authorization Migrations define verified organizations, campaigns, donations, disbursements, confirmations, program submissions, audit entries, administrator roles, PayMongo idempotency, payout destinations, and queued ledger jobs. Row Level Security is enabled on all exposed operational tables. Sensitive mutations use server-only data-access modules and recheck administrator authorization. Private evidence remains in access-controlled Storage; public pages receive only fingerprints and redacted context. Review controls include: - reviewers cannot approve their own submission; - a sole owner override is allowed and permanently logged; - payout destinations require separation between submission and approval; - donations are blocked when no active organization payout destination exists; and - every approval and ledger confirmation enters the administrator audit log. ## PayMongo setup and payment verification 1. Add the matching PayMongo secret key and environment flag. 2. Create `https://YOUR_DOMAIN/api/webhooks/paymongo` in the PayMongo dashboard. 3. Subscribe to `checkout_session.payment.paid`. 4. Store the webhook signing secret in `PAYMONGO_WEBHOOK_SECRET`. 5. Configure an approved PayMongo organization destination for direct settlement. For development payment checks, use PayMongo's documented cards: | Scenario | Card number | Result | | ------------------ | --------------------- | ---------------------------- | | Successful card | `4343 4343 4343 4345` | Payment succeeds without 3DS | | 3D Secure | `4120 0000 0000 0007` | Select **Authorize** | | Insufficient funds | `5100 0000 0000 0198` | Payment is declined | Use any future expiry and any three-digit CVC. After PayMongo redirects back, verify the signed webhook result in the campaign audit trail, **Admin → Transactions**, and **Admin → Blockchain**. Official references: - [Hosted Checkout](https://docs.paymongo.com/docs/payment-channels-hosted-checkout) - [Payment acceptance testing](https://docs.paymongo.com/docs/payment-acceptance-testing) - [Webhooks](https://docs.paymongo.com/docs/creating-a-webhook-endpoint) - [Split Payments](https://docs.paymongo.com/docs/seeds-payment-splitting) ## Solana integrity ledger TrackAid uses Solana's public Memo program rather than a custom token or value-transfer contract. Each successful record contains: - protocol and version identifiers; - record type and UUID; - campaign or submission UUID; - exact PHP amount in integer centavos; - currency `PHP` and `funds: offchain`; and - the SHA-256 payload fingerprint. The dedicated recorder is included as a required memo signer, so the public transaction proves which TrackAid key submitted it. The memo contains no donor name, bank data, PayMongo secret, receipt, or private evidence. TrackAid pays the small Devnet transaction fee; donors need no wallet and no SOL. `ledger_jobs` stores signed Solana transaction signatures before submission and checks previous signatures before retrying. Both queued jobs and public audit entries accept Solana signatures only and open in Solana Explorer. ## Commands | Command | Purpose | | ------------------- | ------------------------- | | `pnpm dev` | Start the development app | | `pnpm build` | Create a production build | | `pnpm start` | Run the production build | | `pnpm typecheck` | Check TypeScript | | `pnpm lint` | Run ESLint | | `pnpm test` | Run Vitest | | `pnpm format:check` | Check formatting | ## Deployment Production deploys from `main` to Vercel. 1. Apply Supabase migrations. 2. Add production environment variables in Vercel; mark signer and provider keys as sensitive. 3. Deploy the exact commit that passed lint, formatting, type checking, tests, and `pnpm build`. 4. Verify PayMongo webhook rejection for invalid signatures and authorization on the scheduled ledger endpoint. 5. Confirm the public recorder address and at least one signed ledger transaction in Solana Explorer. `vercel.json` runs the ledger worker daily. A reconciled PayMongo webhook also attempts one ledger job immediately. ## Security and privacy - Never commit `.env*`, provider keys, webhook secrets, RPC credentials, or signing keys. - Payment details are entered only on PayMongo's hosted page. - Webhook signatures and event IDs are verified before donation state changes. - Amounts are reconciled as integer centavos, never floating-point pesos. - Evidence files remain private; public records expose only redacted details and fingerprints. - Blockchain records prove that a signed value and fingerprint were published, not that an off-chain purchase or delivery was truthful. - Run Supabase security/performance advisors and dependency audits after schema or package changes. Before accepting live donations, complete payment-provider activation and compliance, enable all available Supabase password protections, verify webhook retry behavior, protect the Solana key in managed secrets, and commission an independent security review. ## Development workflow - Preserve existing user and payment data. - Add tests for payment, authorization, reconciliation, and ledger behavior. - Run `pnpm format:check`, `pnpm lint`, `pnpm typecheck`, `pnpm test`, and `pnpm build` before release. - Use Conventional Commits such as `feat:`, `fix:`, `docs:`, `test:`, `refactor:`, or `chore:`. - Never commit generated builds, dependencies, local environments, or credentials.
